content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper addresses an important question regarding a class of language/image models that embed both modalities into a shared vector space, with the embeddings (normally) trained jointly with a contrastive objective. The most famous recent example of this class is CLIP.  This paper investigates an alternative training scheme, in which pretrained models (trained separately for each modality) are adapted for the joint embedding task. 

The reviewers were lukewarm about this paper. The main concerns were limited technical novelty, questions about the scope of evaluation, and overall judgment of impact. The authors addressed all of these in the rebuttal, but unfortunately there was not much of a subsequent discussion. 

I read the paper, the reviews and the responses. Too go over the specific issues brought up:

A. "No technical novelty", "application of existing techniques". This doesn't seem like a real issue to me. A work that shows how to use known techniques better/differently could be much more important than work introducing a new technique that turns out to be a bust. 

B. Insufficient evaluation. I actually think COCO is in itself (barely) sufficient, but the authors report a lot more results in the rebuttal. 

C. "The work might not generalize beyond the specific datasets and tasks reported" - perhaps, but isn't it (not knowing whether it will generalize) true for almost every single empirical paper in the field?
I would consider more heavily a specific concern about a feature of this work that may make it less general, but none were brought up.

D. Similarity to [1] in review by osUw. I agree with the authors that the similarity is superficial.

In my opinion, while indeed the *technical* novelty (introduction of new technical material, like me math, new loss fuction or architecture, etc.) is limited, the contributions are above bar for acceptance. Joint image/language embedding models are at the moment the most promising advancement towards open world image understanding. The cost and complexity of training those models is a significant issue, and the paper provides an interesting component to our emerging understanding of how we may be able to reduce the cost and complexity. It's not perfect, but few papers are.

content.title: Author Response Summary (4 additional datasets + point by point differences to prior work)
content.comment:
## Comparison to LiT on four additional image-text retrieval datasets

| IR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      29.33 |     9.56 |            8.32 | 12.24 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **37.25** |    **14.04** |           **12.07** | **17.58** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |     +4.48% |            +3.75% |  +5.34% |

| TR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      27.75 |    10.71 |            9.61 | 12.67 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **35.67** |    **14.41** |           **11.57** | **17.37** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |      +3.7% |            +1.96 %|   +4.7% |


We show that **LilT significantly improves over LiT's performance for tasks involving more complex linguistic parsing (e.g. image-text retrieval). Additionally, we include more results in the supplement (CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet-Adversarial).** We note that prior work (e.g. LiT) does not test on image-text retrieval tasks, only image classification tasks.
Image-text retrieval is a task that is more general in ways than image-text classification, and can be used to gain a broader idea of how a method performs in a less constrained setting. 

## Differences from prior work
|                          | How to Adapt Your Large-Scale Vision-and-Language Model                          | Our work                                                            |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Setting                  | Finetuning                                                                       | Pretraining                                                   |
| Model                    | CLIP (Already Aligned)                                                           | Unaligned Image / Text Encoders                               |
| Tasks                    | Few-shot                                                                         | 0-shot                                                        |
| Methods                  | Linear Probe, Prompt Tuning, Adapter, Compacter, LN Tuning                       | BitFit, Adapter, Deep Adapter, LN Tuning, LiT                 |
| Evaluation               | Supervised Classification                                                        | Image-Text Retrieval (0-shot),Classification (0-shot)         |
| Training Pairs           | 1-5                                                                              | 500,000 - 1,500,000                                           |
| Datasets                 | MNIST, EuroSAT, CIFAR-10/100, Flowers102, DTD, Food101, WILDS, MiniImageNet, CUB | XD10, Flickr30K, COCO, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-Adversarial, SVHN |
| Multilingual Experiments | No                                                                               | Yes                                                           |



Prior work using adapters [4,5,6] studies parameter efficient methods for _finetuning already trained_-vision language models (finetuning CLIP), we study parameter efficient methods for _pretraining unaligned_ image and text encoders (creating CLIP). The only prior work on _parameter-efficient vision-language pretraining_ is LiT, which proposes to freeze the image encoder, achieving a reduction of 50% trainable parameters. We achieve a reduction of 93%, and show that LiT-style training appears to results in worse performance for image-text retrieval, in contrast to our method. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed study on the combination and interactions of various parameter-efficient techniques for _pretraining_, in contrast to prior work on adapters for VL and parameter-efficient pretraining. 

## Summary of Contributions
-  By _updating only 7% of parameters, we achieve significantly better (~5\% avg. absolute improvements) across 5 image-text retrieval tasks relative to LiT training (50% of parameters)_.
- In a multilingual setting, **LilT can zero-shot transfer from a high-resource language to a low-resource language more effectively than CLIP or LiT**, increasing the capability of image-text retrieval models to operate for low resource languages without additional training -- _a societally important use case_. 
- We show that _training 0.31% of parameters is sufficient to achieve nearly equivalent performance to training 100% of parameters_ for classification tasks.
- A detailed empirical study of the interactions between various methods for parameter-efficient transfer learning.

content.title: Batch size and prompt tuning and additional experiments
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. We address your comments below, and hope that you take these into account in picking a new recommendation for our paper. 


**Influence of batch size:** As you noted, batch size is known to influence contrastive learning. We find that larger batches result in consistently improved performance (up to a batch size of 512, which is the highest we were able to test). However, we test the performance of all models using the same batch size, for fairness of comparison. Another benefit of our method is _significantly_ reduced memory cost. Finally, from a practical perspective, the training speed is also decreased. For 500k pairs, training a `base` sized model takes $\approx 20$h with LilT and $\approx 29$h with CLIP, which is speed increase of roughly $30$\%.

**Prompt-Tuning:** Surprisingly, we find that standard prompt-tuning did not work for contrastive vision-language alignment. We speculate that this is partially due to the importance of layerwise adaptation in transformers -- it may be necessary to tune the parameters in each layer, whereas prompt tuning effectively only "tunes" a set of parameters before the first layer. Another obstacle to prompt tuning may be that the text and image encoders require adaptation at different parts of the transformer stack (Fig 4), whereas prompt tuning attempts to adapt the inputs (with parameters corresponding to a new pseudo-"layer" below the lowermost layer of the transformer stack) at the same level for both encoders. 


**Additional Datasets** We add experiments on four additional image-text retrieval datasets to strengthen our conclusions. 
| IR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      29.33 |     9.56 |            8.32 | 12.24 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **37.25** |    **14.04** |           **12.07** | **17.58** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |     +4.48% |            +3.75% |  +5.34% |

| TR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      27.75 |    10.71 |            9.61 | 12.67 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **35.67** |    **14.41** |           **11.57** | **17.37** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |      +3.7% |            +1.96 %|   +4.7% |

We show that LiT-style training, while effective for image classification, experiences degraded performance for image-text retrieval tasks, which require more complex language understanding. In contrast, the proposed method (LilT) does not experience this degradation while also requiring fewer parameters ($7$\% vs $50$\%) to be updated.

content.title: Experiments on four additional datasets
content.comment:
We appreciate the review, and address your comments. We hope our response can convince you in making a new recommendation for our work. 

**Strength of Testbed** We note that prior work (e.g. LiT) does not test on image-text retrieval tasks, only image classification tasks.
Image-text retrieval is a task that is more general in ways than image-text classification, and can be used to gain a broader idea of how a method performs in a less constrained setting. 
In our paper, **we add image-text retrieval tasks to the testbench**. The datasets we use for testing image-text retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k) are the same as other recent papers for VL pretraining [1,2,3]. 
On these datasets, we show that LiT's performance on image-text retrieval is degraded relative to CLIP, whereas our approach (LilT) does not experience this degradation. 
However, **we add results for four more image-text retrieval datasets below, in addition to the COCO and Flickr30k results in the paper**.

| IR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      29.33 |     9.56 |            8.32 | 12.24 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **37.25** |    **14.04** |           **12.07** | **17.58** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |     +4.48% |            +3.75% |  +5.34% |

| TR Mean         | Winoground | Concadia | VizWiz-Captions | CC3M  |
|-----------------|------------|----------|-----------------|-------|
| LiT             |      27.75 |    10.71 |            9.61 | 12.67 |
| LilT (Ours)     |      **35.67** |    **14.41** |           **11.57** | **17.37** |
| Absolute % Gain |       +7.92% |      +3.7% |            +1.96 %|   +4.7% |


This shows that LilT can improve upon LiT's performance for tasks involving more complex linguistic parsing (e.g. image-text retrieval). Additionally, we include more results in the supplement (CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet-Adversarial).

**Technical  / Empirical Novelty:** Prior work using adapters [4,5,6] studies parameter efficient methods for _finetuning already trained_-vision language models (finetuning CLIP), we study parameter efficient methods for _pretraining unaligned_ image and text encoders (creating CLIP). The only prior work on _parameter-efficient vision-language pretraining_ is LiT, which proposes to freeze the image encoder, achieving a reduction of 50% trainable parameters. We achieve a reduction of 93%, and show that LiT-style training appears to results in worse performance for image-text retrieval, in contrast to our method. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed study on the combination and interactions of various parameter-efficient techniques for _pretraining_, in contrast to prior work on adapters for VL and parameter-efficient pretraining. 


We hope you can consider these additional experiments and reconsider your score. We look forward to your response.

content.title: Significant differences between our work and prior work
content.comment:
We believe there may be severe misunderstandings of our work, as well as possible missed key results. We correct them below, and hope that this leads you to consider a different recommendation for our work. 

**Weakness #1: There are very few similarities to "How to Adapt Your Large-Scale Vision-and-Language Model"**: We both use adapters, but so do many other papers. They are just a technology we consider to achieve parameter efficiency. There are very few similarities between our setting and the setting of "How to Adapt Your Large-Scale Vision-and-Language Model". We summarize the differences in the table below. 


|                          | How to Adapt Your Large-Scale Vision-and-Language Model                          | Our work                                                            |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Setting                  | Finetuning                                                                       | Pretraining                                                   |
| Model                    | CLIP (Already Aligned)                                                           | Unaligned Image / Text Encoders                               |
| Tasks                    | Few-shot                                                                         | 0-shot                                                        |
| Methods                  | Linear Probe, Prompt Tuning, Adapter, Compacter, LN Tuning                       | BitFit, Adapter, Deep Adapter, LN Tuning, LiT                 |
| Evaluation               | Supervised Classification                                                        | Image-Text Retrieval (0-shot),Classification (0-shot)         |
| Training Pairs           | 1-5                                                                              | 500,000 - 1,500,000                                           |
| Datasets                 | MNIST, EuroSAT, CIFAR-10/100, Flowers102, DTD, Food101, WILDS, MiniImageNet, CUB | XD10, Flickr30K, COCO, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-Adversarial, SVHN |
| Multilingual Experiments | No                                                                               | Yes                                                           |

The setting is completely different (use an _already trained CLIP_ for classification with 1-5 labeled samples vs _create CLIP_ in a parameter-efficient way with large scale training), the target task is completely different (zero-shot image-text retrieval vs few-shot classification), the baseline models are different (an already trained CLIP model vs unaligned image and text models) and we even consider different technologies (adapters and layer norms are the only commonalities), and the datasets are different. 

**Weakness #2: Empirical findings are not significant enough, although we achieve an order of magnitude reduction in trainable parameters relative to prior work**. We show that _training 0.31% of parameters is sufficient to achieve nearly equivalent performance to training 100% of parameters_. By _training 7% of parameters, we achieve significantly better (9-10% absolute improvement) on image-text retrieval relative to LiT training (50% of parameters)_. **If this is not significant for you, what types of numbers would you consider significant?**


**Weakness #3: Is it interesting that contrastive vision-language models created with parameter-efficient transfer learning conserve useful existing knowledge?**
 We think think this conclusion is surprising and interesting, as do the other reviewers. It is true that techniques for parameter-efficient finetuning such as adapters exist. The existence of those techniques does not imply by logical necessity that those techniques will be successful in aligning a language model and image model, as previous techniques such as LiT require training all the parameters of the text encoder. Moreover, your statement is missing context from the paper. **We show that the knowledge conservation of parameter-efficient training is particularly helpful in a multilingual language model, as the image-text alignment in a high-resource language propagates better to low-resource languages compared to full-model training.  This is not obvious, and has an important, real-world use case.**



We hope this can clear up confusion regarding our paper and main claims. We look forward to your response.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper shows the good efficiency and effect of parameter-efficient contrastive vision-language alignment through transfer learning. Specifically, contrastive vision-language models can be created by updating a small set of parameters of pretrained vision models(e.g. DeiT) and pretrained language models(e.g. SimCSE).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

[+] experiment results demonstrate contrastive vision-language models can be created by updates to a relatively small (<7%) set of parameters in pretrained vision and language models, which is a very practical idea.

[+] empirical study illustrates contrastive vision-language models created with parameter-efficient transfer learning conserve useful existing knowledge from their initializations better than full model finetuning

Weaknesses

[-] As the authors claimed in the Limitation section, the conclusions of this work are limited to the datasets, model structure, and downstream tasks.

[-] It is known that batch size plays a key role in contrastive learning. I am curious about the influence of different batch size on your conclusion.

[-] parameter-efficient transfer learning is a hot but not a new topic. Except for Adapter and Unlocking, there are other methods such as Prompt-tuning. Not all parameter-efficient transfer learning methods work for contrastive alignment may be another limitation.

[-] In the Abstract, "vision-language models" and "vision and language model" may make readers confused

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of efficient fine tuning vision language models. Specifically, the authors seek to answer the following question: "given that strong, pre-trained vision and language models both exist, can we minimally update both of their parameters to align their representations?". The authors adopted the following options 1) initializing the vision and language encoders from pre-trained ones, 2) locking their params, 3) unlocking some of the params and 4) insert a trainable modules (adapters). They showed that by fine tuning just 7% of the parameters, they were able to match the performance of the full fine tuning strategy on retrieval (Flickr) and zero-shot classification (ImageNet)
content.strength_and_weaknesses: [Strength] The authors conducted many experiments to answer various research questions such as multilingual adaptation and alignment effects. They also did extensive zero-shot experiments comparing with corresponding baselines.[Weakness] This paper is not technically novel and the ideas are simple. It is an incremental step from LiT and from fine tuning approaches that use adapters before. In addition, as stated in the papers, it has a limited set up, which include 1) only testing with COCO dataset, and later 1.5M image-text pairs. It might not work for other datasets, 2) only focusing on zero-shot classification and retrieval tasks. Their conclusions might not hold for other downstream problems, 3) only testing on transformer architecture, which in my opinion, is not a main limitation, however.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient contrastive vision-language method by leveraging a pre-trained vision encoder and a text encoder. The key idea is to align a well-trained vision encoder and a text encoder by updating a small percentage of their parameters on a small-scale pre-training dataset. The proposed method can achieve comparable performance as full-model training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) requires a huge amount of computational resources, which is not affordable by a lot of researchers. Therefore, it is important to design a parameter-efficient training strategy without sacrificing the model performance.
2. The proposed method is simple and can be easily applied to existing methods.

Weakness:
1. The proposed method is quite similar to [1]. Although [1] is designed for fine-tuning CLIP on downstream tasks, these two works share a lot of technical solutions (e.g., layerNorm tuning and adding adapters).
2. This paper is more like an empirical study (combination of existing techniques). The technical novelty and contribution is limited, and new empirical findings are not significant enough.
3. One contribution of this paper is “we show that contrastive vision-language models created with parameter-efficient transfer learning conserve useful existing knowledge from their initializations better than full model finetuning”. This conclusion is obvious. Since parameter-efficient training freezes most of the parameters of the well-trained vision/text encoder, this training obviously will keep existing knowledge.

[1] How to Adapt Your Large-Scale Vision-and-Language Model
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-organized and easy to follow. The quality is good but the novelty and technical contribution is quite limited. Since the proposed method is simple, it shouldn’t be hard to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a simple parameter-efficient training method for contrative vision-language pre-training. Although the problem is important and some interesting finds are observed, the technical novelty and contribution are not significant enough.

content.title: Contrastive Alignment of Vision to Language Through Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning
content.TL;DR: Changing a small number (<7%) of parameters in already trained language and image models can match the performance of full model training for creating CLIP-like models.
content.abstract:
Contrastive vision-language models (e.g. CLIP) are typically created by updating all the parameters of a vision model and language model through contrastive training. Can such models be created by a small number of parameter updates to an already-trained language model and vision model? The literature describes techniques that can create vision-language models by updating a small number of parameters in a language model, but these require already aligned visual representations and are non-contrastive, hence unusable for latency-sensitive applications such as neural search. We explore the feasibility and benefits of parameter-efficient contrastive vision-language alignment through transfer learning: creating a model such as CLIP by minimally updating an already-trained vision and language model. We find that a minimal set of parameter updates ($<$7\%) can achieve the same performance as full-model training, and updating specific components ($<$1\% of parameters) can match 75\% of full-model training. We describe a series of experiments: we show that existing knowledge is conserved more strongly in parameter-efficient training and that parameter-efficient scaling scales with model and dataset size. Where paired-image text data is scarce but strong multilingual language models exist (e.g. low resource languages), parameter-efficient training is even preferable to full-model training. Given a fixed compute budget, parameter-efficient training allows training larger models on the same hardware, achieving equivalent performance in less time. Parameter-efficient training hence constitutes an energy-efficient and effective training strategy for contrastive vision-language models that may be preferable to the full-model training paradigm for common use cases.
Code and weights at https://github.com/codezakh/LilT.
